reference.text: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., CRC Press, 2013, chapters 1–2.
content.0: Suppose we want to estimate the probability $p$ that a coin lands heads. Before tossing it, we are uncertain about $p$, though we may have some prior information. After observing several tosses, we update that uncertainty.
content.1: Bayesian inference combines what we knew before collecting data with what the new data tell us. A prior distribution represents uncertainty about an unknown parameter before observing the data; the posterior distribution represents uncertainty after the data are observed.

content.9: Suppose a coin is equally likely to be fair or double-headed. Let $H$ be the hypothesis that it is double-headed. Before a toss, $P(H)=1/2$. If heads is observed, $P(\text{heads}\mid H)=1$ and $P(\text{heads}\mid H^c)=1/2$.
content.11: The observation raises the probability of the double-headed hypothesis from one half to two thirds. The next page extends this idea to a continuous parameter.
